why_how.text: Driver assistance systems help with tasks like lane keeping and blind spots, but they do not drive the vehicle by themselves.
Most warning systems are passive, so the driver may still have to act after a warning.
Cameras and back-up warnings help while backing, but mirror and shoulder checks are still required.
A blind spot monitor warns of vehicles beside you, but the lane-change checks stay with the driver.

scenario.text: A driver backs out of a driveway in a car with a rear camera and a back-up warning.

reasoning.text: A rear camera does not replace mirror and over-the-shoulder checks, and a back-up warning still requires mirrors, a shoulder look and any camera.

result.text: The driver uses the camera and the warning, and also checks the mirrors and looks over the shoulder while backing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a rear camera replaces looking over your shoulder when backing.

correction.text: A rear camera shows the area behind the vehicle but does not replace mirror and over-the-shoulder checks.

prompt.text: A car's blind spot monitor shows no warning before a lane change. What should the driver still do?

answer.text: Check the mirrors and look over the shoulder.

rationale.text: A blind spot monitor warns of vehicles in the blind spots, but you must still check mirrors and look over your shoulder before a lane change.

lines.text: They do not drive the car.

narration.text: This lesson begins the chapter on advanced driver assistance systems. These systems help with tasks such as staying in the lane, avoiding crashes, covering blind spots and keeping a space cushion, but they do not drive the vehicle by themselves. We will start with warning systems, which alert the driver by sound, light or vibration, and then look at back-up warnings, blind spot monitors, rear, side and surround-view cameras, and curve speed warnings. For each one, notice what the system does and what the driver is still required to do.

lines.text: Alerts by sound, light or vibration.
The driver may still have to act.

narration.text: Vehicle warning systems alert the driver by sound, light or vibration that a crash is about to happen or that something has malfunctioned. Warning technologies exist mainly to alert the driver in specific situations. Most warning systems are passive: they warn of a possible problem but do not stop the crash themselves, so the driver may still have to act. In other words, a warning is information, not protection. When an alert sounds, the response, whether braking, steering or checking around the vehicle, still comes from the person behind the wheel.

lines.text: Back-up warning: sensors behind the car.
Blind spot monitor: symbol, sound or vibration.
Mirrors and shoulder checks still required.

narration.text: A back-up warning uses sensors behind the vehicle once you shift into reverse and alerts you by sound, vibration or both, yet you must still check mirrors, look over your shoulder and use any camera while backing. A blind spot monitor warns of vehicles in your blind spots with a symbol, sound or vibration, sometimes more strongly when you signal, but you must still check mirrors and look over your shoulder before a lane change. Both systems add a warning to your own checks; neither one removes the need to look for yourself before you move the car.

lines.text: Rear camera turns on in reverse.
Sideview camera shows the next lane.
Use both with mirrors and head checks.

narration.text: A rear camera turns on when you shift into reverse to show the area behind the vehicle, but it does not replace mirror and over-the-shoulder checks while backing. Depending on the vehicle, the rear camera picture may show up in the rearview mirror, the sun visor, the center console screen or another spot. A sideview camera shows an enlarged video view of the lane beside you when you signal or switch it on, works much like a blind spot monitor, and should be used together with mirrors and head checks. Some newer vehicles use sideview cameras instead of traditional side mirrors.

lines.text: Cameras in the bumper and mirrors.
Curve warnings: you set the speed.

narration.text: A surround-view or around-view monitor helps with parking by showing a virtual bird's-eye view of the vehicle and nearby curbs, markings and cars, and it too should be used along with mirrors and head checks. In most surround-view systems one camera sits in the middle of the front bumper and two more look down from the side mirrors, and some add audio warnings when you get too close to an obstacle. A curve speed warning alerts you by sound, vibration or both when you approach a curve or exit too fast, but you remain responsible for choosing a safe speed.

title.text: A camera is not a look

lines.text: Rear camera does not replace checks.
Back-up warning does not replace checks.
Mirrors and shoulder looks every time.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A rear camera or a back-up warning can make backing feel fully covered. The handbook says otherwise. A rear camera does not replace mirror and over-the-shoulder checks while backing, and a back-up warning still requires you to check mirrors, look over your shoulder and use any camera. The same is true of a blind spot monitor before a lane change. When a question asks what a driver must still do in a car with these systems, the answer is the ordinary checks: the mirrors, the look over the shoulder, and the camera if the car has one.

lines.text: The blind spot monitor is quiet.
What must the driver still do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: before a lane change, a car's blind spot monitor shows no warning. What should the driver still do? Recall what the handbook says about the monitor before reading on. The driver must still check the mirrors and look over the shoulder. A blind spot monitor warns of vehicles in the blind spots with a symbol, sound or vibration, sometimes more strongly when you signal, but it does not replace your own checks before a lane change. A quiet monitor is information, and the driver's own look is still required.

To review, driver assistance systems help with lane keeping, avoiding crashes, blind spots and space cushions, but they do not drive the vehicle by themselves. Warning systems alert by sound, light or vibration, and most are passive, so the driver may still have to act. Back-up warnings, blind spot monitors and rear, side and surround-view cameras all add information, but you must still check mirrors and look over your shoulder. A curve speed warning alerts you when you approach a curve or exit too fast, and choosing a safe speed remains your responsibility.

why_how.text: Detection systems and collision warnings alert you to people, objects and other vehicles, but they do not replace your own attention.
Each warning sounds or looks different, so knowing them tells you what the car is reporting.
Detection systems work at low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour.

scenario.text: A driver pulling into a tight parking space hears the parking sensors change to a constant tone.

reasoning.text: Parking sensors signal how close objects are as you park, and a constant tone means you are too close to an object.

result.text: The driver stops and adjusts, because the constant tone means the car is too close to an object.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a forward collision warning will brake the car for you.

correction.text: A forward collision warning scans ahead and warns you so you can brake or swerve, but the warning alone does not brake.

memory_support.text: Faster beeps closer, constant tone too close.

prompt.text: At what kind of speed does pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection generally work?

answer.text: Low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour.

rationale.text: Pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection works at low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour, and some versions brake automatically.

narration.text: This lesson covers systems that detect people, objects and other vehicles and then warn you. We will look at pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection and how its beeps work, forward collision warnings, lane departure warnings, parking sensors, rear cross-traffic alerts and high speed alerts. Each of these systems tells the driver something, but none of them in this lesson takes over the driving. Do not rely on bicycle, pedestrian or obstacle detection; keep checking for people and objects yourself, especially in urban areas.

lines.text: Works at low speeds, about twenty-five.

narration.text: Pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection works at low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour, and some versions brake automatically. Some detection systems only notice cyclists, pedestrians or obstacles directly in front of the vehicle and moving the same way, so read the owner's manual to learn how your car warns you. With detection systems, beeps may speed up as the vehicle gets closer to an obstacle, and continuous beeping can mean a collision is imminent. Do not rely on these systems; keep checking for people and objects yourself, especially in urban areas.

lines.text: Forward collision warning does not brake.

narration.text: A forward collision warning scans ahead and warns of slower or stopped vehicles and objects so you can brake or swerve in time, but the warning alone does not brake for you. A lane departure warning uses visual, vibrating or sound alerts to tell you that you are drifting out of your lane so you can steer back to its center. A lane departure warning leaves the steering to you: its alerts exist to prompt the driver to steer back toward the middle of the lane after an accidental drift. Both of these systems warn, and the driver does the braking or steering.

Parking sensors signal how close objects are as you park; a constant tone means you are too close to an object. A rear cross-traffic alert warns you when one or more vehicles are about to cross the path you are backing into. A high speed alert sounds when you are speeding, helping you hold a safe speed. These alerts cover three different moments: easing into a parking space, backing out into a lane or parking aisle, and holding a steady speed on the road. In each case the system speaks up, and the driver decides what to do next.

lines.text: A forward collision warning only warns.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A forward collision warning sounds so urgent that drivers sometimes assume the car will stop itself. The warning alone does not brake for you; it warns of slower or stopped vehicles and objects so that you can brake or swerve in time. Detection beeps work the same way: faster beeps mean you are getting closer, and continuous beeping can mean a collision is imminent, so the response is yours. When a question asks what a warning system does, the answer is that it alerts; when it asks who acts, the answer is the driver.

lines.text: At what speeds does it work?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: at what kind of speed does pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection generally work? Recall the figure before reading on. It works at low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour, and some versions brake automatically. Some systems only notice cyclists, pedestrians or obstacles directly in front of the vehicle and moving the same way, which is why the handbook says to read the owner's manual. And whatever your car has, do not rely on it; keep checking for people and objects yourself, especially in urban areas.

Let us sum up. Pedestrian, bicycle and obstacle detection works at low speeds, generally around twenty-five miles per hour, its beeps speed up as you close in, and continuous beeping can mean a collision is imminent. Do not rely on it; keep checking yourself, especially in urban areas. A forward collision warning alerts you but does not brake, and a lane departure warning tells you that you are drifting while leaving the steering to you. A constant parking-sensor tone means too close, a rear cross-traffic alert warns of cars crossing your backing path, and a high speed alert sounds when you are speeding.

why_how.text: Some technologies perform part of the driving task, either adjusting the vehicle or helping you brake or steer.
Knowing which systems act on their own, and which only warn, tells you what to expect in an emergency.

scenario.text: A driver looks away as traffic ahead stops suddenly, in a car with automatic emergency braking.

reasoning.text: Automatic emergency braking senses slow or stopped traffic ahead and brakes hard if the driver does not respond.

result.text: The system may brake, but the driver should keep scanning and keep a safe following distance anyway.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking lane keeping assist works on every road.

correction.text: Lane keeping assist does not work when lane lines are faint or covered by snow or dirt, and a nudge of the wheel cancels it.

memory_support.text: Warning tells, assist acts, driver still decides.

prompt.text: Your car brakes on its own while you back toward an obstacle you did not notice. Which system did that?

rationale.text: Automatic reverse braking warns with beeps or visual signals when an obstacle is detected while backing and applies the brakes at once if the driver does not react.

narration.text: This lesson covers technologies that do more than warn. Driver assistance technologies perform part of the driving task in certain situations, either adjusting the vehicle themselves or helping the driver brake or steer. Safety-critical technologies are those that may prevent a crash or reduce how severe it is. We will look at automatic emergency braking, automatic reverse braking, lane keeping assist and left turn crash avoidance, how each compares with the warning-only systems, and what the handbook says about these technologies during a practical driving test.

lines.text: Both act if you do not.

narration.text: Automatic emergency braking senses slow or stopped traffic or objects ahead and brakes hard if the driver does not respond, so keep scanning and keep a safe following distance anyway. Automatic reverse braking warns with beeps or visual signals when an obstacle is detected while backing and applies the brakes at once if the driver does not react. Both systems give the driver the first chance to act and then step in. That is the key difference from a warning-only system, which alerts you and leaves every action to you, including the braking.

lines.text: Lane keeping may steer you back.
Faint or covered lines stop it.
Left turn assist watches oncoming traffic.

narration.text: Lane keeping assist alerts you when you drift and may gently steer you back if you do not act; a nudge of the wheel cancels it, and it does not work when lane lines are faint or covered by snow or dirt. Left turn crash avoidance watches oncoming traffic during low-speed left turns, can stop the car from moving into a gap that is too small, and brakes automatically if a crash is imminent, but you must still judge when it is safe to turn. Each of these systems helps in a narrow situation, and the driver stays responsible for every decision.

lines.text: Cross-traffic alert warns; reverse braking brakes.

narration.text: Here is the trap: pairs of systems that sound alike. A forward collision warning only warns and leaves the braking to you, whereas automatic emergency braking applies the brakes itself if you fail to respond. A rear cross-traffic alert only warns that a vehicle is about to cross your backing path, whereas automatic reverse braking applies the brakes itself when you fail to react to a detected obstacle. When a question names a system, ask whether it is a warning or an assist. The word alert or warning usually means the driver acts; braking means the car can act.

lines.text: Technology can react faster than you.
The examiner decides how it is scored.

narration.text: Assistance technology can react faster than a person when a vehicle or object suddenly appears ahead, and if that happens during a practical driving test, the examiner decides at their discretion how it is scored. So the road test does not ignore these systems, but it does not treat them as automatic passes or failures either. The examiner looks at what happened and decides. The rest of the test still measures your own driving: your scanning, your speed, your following distance and your judgment at turns, which no assistance system replaces.

Here is a quick check: you are backing toward an obstacle you did not notice, and the car brakes on its own. Which system did that? Name it before reading on. That was automatic reverse braking. It warns with beeps or visual signals when an obstacle is detected while backing and applies the brakes at once if the driver does not react. A rear cross-traffic alert, by comparison, only warns that a vehicle is about to cross your backing path; it does not brake. The braking system gives you the first chance to stop, then acts if you do not.

lines.text: They act only when you do not.

narration.text: To sum up, driver assistance technologies perform part of the driving task in certain situations, and safety-critical ones may prevent a crash or reduce its severity. Automatic emergency braking brakes hard for slow or stopped traffic if you do not respond, and automatic reverse braking stops the car while backing if you do not react. Lane keeping assist may gently steer you back, but not on faint or covered lines, and left turn crash avoidance can stop a risky turn while you still judge the gap. On the road test, the examiner decides how a sudden assisted reaction is scored.

why_how.text: Convenience features make driving easier, but they are not permitted during the testing process.
Nevada law defines which vehicles count as autonomous by their level of driving automation.

scenario.text: An applicant plans to use adaptive cruise control during the drive test to keep a steady gap.

reasoning.text: Convenience technologies such as adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking are not permitted during the testing process.

result.text: The applicant must drive the test without adaptive cruise control.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any car with some automation counts as autonomous under Nevada law.

correction.text: Nevada counts a vehicle as autonomous only when its automated driving system is designed for level three, four or five.

memory_support.text: Levels three to five drive themselves.

prompt.text: Under what conditions does the handbook advise against using adaptive cruise control?

answer.text: In bad weather and other unsafe conditions.

rationale.text: Adaptive cruise control holds a following gap you choose, but you must stay aware, and it is advised not to use it in bad weather or other unsafe conditions.

narration.text: This lesson covers the convenience technologies in the handbook and Nevada's definition of an autonomous vehicle. Convenience technologies such as adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking do not demonstrate a required skill and are not permitted during the testing process. We will look at how adaptive cruise control is set up and when to avoid it, what automatic parallel parking does and what stays the driver's job, and then the levels of driving automation, including which levels make a vehicle autonomous under Nevada law.

lines.text: Holds a following gap you choose.

narration.text: Adaptive cruise control speeds up or slows down to hold a following gap you choose, but you must stay aware of your surroundings, and it is advised not to use it in bad weather or other unsafe conditions. To use adaptive cruise control, reach your desired speed, switch it on and choose a short, medium or long following gap; advanced versions can slow, stop and restart in traffic jams. Even with the system holding the gap, the driver remains the one watching the road and deciding when to take back control. It assists; you drive.

lines.text: Prompts: pull ahead, reverse, hands off.
You brake and watch around you.

narration.text: Automatic parallel parking searches for a usable space and guides you into it with prompts such as pulling ahead, shifting to reverse and letting go of the wheel, but you remain responsible for braking and watching around you. Together with adaptive cruise control, it is one of the convenience technologies that do not demonstrate a required skill and are not permitted during the testing process. So on the drive test, you park by yourself, and anywhere else, the system may steer while you keep your foot ready and your eyes on the surroundings.

Here is the trap. A car's convenience features can feel like part of good driving, so applicants may expect to use them on the test. They may not. Convenience technologies such as adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking do not demonstrate a required skill and are not permitted during the testing process. That is different from safety systems that react on their own to a sudden hazard, where the examiner decides at their discretion how the event is scored. So convenience features stay off, while sudden safety reactions are judged case by case.

lines.text: SAE scale runs zero to five.

narration.text: In Nevada, an autonomous vehicle is one with an automated driving system designed for driving-automation level three, four or five under the SAE J3016 standard, including fully autonomous vehicles. The Society of Automotive Engineers classifies driving automation in levels from zero to five, starting with vehicles that lack the technology and ending with self-driving vehicles. So the lower levels, zero to two, are not autonomous vehicles under Nevada law, even if the car has helpful assistance features. Only the top three levels count.

Here is a quick check: when is it advised not to use adaptive cruise control? Recall the handbook's advice before reading on. It is advised not to use it in bad weather or other unsafe conditions. Adaptive cruise control speeds up or slows down to hold the following gap you choose, but you must stay aware of your surroundings at all times. Remember too that it is a convenience technology, so it is not permitted during the testing process. In normal conditions it can hold the gap, and in poor conditions the driver handles the speed directly.

lines.text: Convenience features stay off on the test.
Autonomous means levels three to five.

narration.text: To wrap up the chapter, convenience technologies such as adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking do not demonstrate a required skill and are not permitted during the testing process. Adaptive cruise control holds a following gap you choose, short, medium or long, and is best avoided in bad weather or other unsafe conditions. Automatic parallel parking finds a space and gives prompts, but you remain responsible for braking and watching around you. In Nevada an autonomous vehicle is designed for level three, four or five on the automation scale that runs from zero to five.
